query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introduce a minor addition of aluminum (~2–3 at.%) into the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy to promote the in situ formation of a protective and adherent alumina (Al₂O₃) scale during high‐temperature exposure without disrupting the BCC solid-solution microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy with well‐balanced room-temperature tensile ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C) but lacking sufficient oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Alloy modification by adding 2–3 at.% Al during melting/casting, ensuring homogeneous distribution.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 800–1000 °C for durations around 5 hours under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: An in situ formed, continuous, slow-growing, and adherent Al₂O₃ surface layer that impedes oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: Due to its high oxygen affinity, the minor Al addition preferentially oxidizes to form a dense and protective alumina film that passivates the alloy surface. Prior studies in similar refractory alloy systems (e.g., PMC6356250 evidence) indicate that limited Al can form stable α-Al₂O₃ scales without significantly altering the bulk BCC phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved oxygen resistance with reduced oxidation kinetics and minimal scale spallation at high temperature while preserving the original ductility and yield strength ranges.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr that exhibits rapid oxidation (pesting) in high-temperature air.
generation.boundary: Valid for isothermal oxidation conditions up to 1000 °C and exposure durations around 5 hours; behavior under intensive thermal cycling or prolonged exposure remains to be established.
generation.uncertainty: While literature supports alumina-scale formation in similar systems, the exact optimum Al content and long-term adhesion under cyclic thermal loads remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples, one with 2–3 at.% Al and one without. Expose both sets in air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, evaluate the oxide scale using SEM/EDS and XRD, and perform mechanical testing at room temperature and 1000 °C.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness, continuity, and phase composition (confirmation of α-Al₂O₃)
Room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloys do not exhibit a significantly lower oxidation rate or if their mechanical properties are degraded relative to the undoped alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The intermetallic compounds of the Ti–Al system are known not to pest []. Aluminium rich TiAl, and the TiAl2 and TiAl3 aluminides can form alumina scales but Al poor TiAl and Ti3Al form titania rich scales and oxidise at much higher rates []. For example, when TiAl with 50 at.% Al was oxidised in air at 950, 1100 and 1200 °C, at the two higher temperatures TiO2 scale formed and there was internal oxidation. Parabolic oxidation kinetics were followed at the low temperature where the oxidation was independent of specimen preparation and fabrication method []. Furthermore, the alloying of TiAl with Nb promoted the formation of continuous alumina scale on TiAl (50 at.% Al) at 950 °C independent of surface preparation or exposure environment (air or O2) but the alloying with Hf had a minimal effect []. The alloying of TiAl with Si improved oxidation resistance []. For Al poor TiAl it is known that the addition of 4 to 12 at.% Nb in Ti–48Al increased oxidation resistance at 850 °C and that the alloys developed continuous bands of dense alumina beneath titania rich surface layer that formed during the early stages of oxidation []. cited_evidence.text: With Nb and Al as constituent elements of the alloys to be designed the oxidation of intermetallic compounds in the Nb–Al binary system also was considered. NbAl3, which is isomorphous with TiAl3, is the only compound in the Nb–Al system that can form continuous αAl2O3 scale at high temperatures [] but it is known to pest, with the worst behaviour exhibited between 650 and 850 °C []. Unlike TiAl3, the NbAl3 aluminide has a narrow solubility range. Like the TiAl3, the depletion of Al by the initial formation of the oxide layer results in the formation of a lower compound, namely Nb2Al, beneath the scale. The latter compound influences the structure, stability and adherence of the oxide layer. Nb2Al cannot form continuous alumina. Rupture of the initial alumina layer is followed by the rapid growth of AlNbO4 and Nb2O5 and the consumption of Nb2Al, which is then followed by the growth of alumina again on the NbAl3. Repetition of this process results in a layered scale and nearly linear oxidation kinetics. Excess Al prevents the formation of the layered structure but degrades the long term oxidation resistance, because of Al evaporation and alumina growth in grain boundaries. However,

The development of oxidation resistance in an alloy requires the presence of an alloying addition that oxidises selectively to produce a protective oxide. The latter requires the oxide to be more stable than that of the base metal. Therefore, a necessary but not sufficient requirement for the formation of a protective oxide on the surface on an alloy is that the oxide is more stable than all possible oxides. Al2O3 and SiO2 are highly stable oxides owing to their low standard free energies of formation and are desirable for oxidation protection at T > 1000 °C. In terms of the standard free energy of oxide formation, the oxides of Nb and Ti are nearly as stable as Al2O3 and SiO2. Which oxide is stable on an alloy also depends on metal activities. Changes in the activities of the elements of an alloy can change the composition of oxidation products significantly. For the oxide of an element to form, the latter must be available at the oxide/alloy or alloy/gas interface and the partial pressure of oxygen in contact with the alloy must exceed the equilibrium pressure for the oxidising reaction at that value of the activity of the element.
